entry.title: recurcast: Coherent Forecasts for History-Dependent Recurrent and Terminal Events in R

link.title: recurcast: Coherent Forecasts for History-Dependent Recurrent and Terminal Events in R

entry.content: Researchers studying recurrent events and terminal outcomes need software that connects incomplete event histories to interpretable forecasts and uncertainty estimates. We present recurcast, an R package for fitting history-dependent recurrent and terminal event models, predicting future event burden and terminal-event risk, and assessing sensitivity to incomplete observation. Users supply event histories, covariates and observation information; the package returns fitted models, dynamic forecasts, uncertainty summaries and diagnostic measures under explicitly stated assumptions. The package integrates over event histories compatible with tied dates or observation windows and supports several frailty distributions for between-subject heterogeneity. A shared probability model generates recurrent-event counts, terminal-event probabilities and restricted mean time alive. Cross-fitted targeting provides influence-function diagnostics and asymptotic inference in supported missing-at-random and right-censoring settings. Separate sensitivity analyses provide bounds under specified recording restrictions. A baseline binary-treatment interface estimates standardized treatment contrasts under consistency, conditional exchangeability, positivity and independent censoring. A C++17 computational core supports the R interface. Independent numerical checks, computational benchmarks, simulation experiments and reproducible examples document accuracy, performance and inferential limitations. Outputs retain observation assumptions, convergence information and numerical diagnostics. The package, tutorials and replication materials are publicly available, supporting transparent analysis across clinical and other event-history applications.

entry.title: How Fast Stored Household Assignments Go Stale: Evidence from North Carolina Voter Rolls

link.title: How Fast Stored Household Assignments Go Stale: Evidence from North Carolina Voter Rolls

entry.content: Household files and identity graphs are judged by whether they still find the person. That test misses what they store. A household assignment can go stale while every person-level link in it stays right, because the people around the person change. We measure how fast, for households derived from a voter register, by following North Carolina registrants on a persistent identifier across 40 distinct snapshots from November 2008 to November 2026 (3.6 million clients at the 2016 build in 60 counties). Eight years after the 2016 build, the graph finds the address of 0.831 of registrants still listed, yet its household is exactly right for only 0.322 of those found (0.309 reading stale listings as departures). entry.title: Decision support framework for mitigating failure demand in healthcare

link.title: Decision support framework for mitigating failure demand in healthcare

entry.content: Failure demand studies in healthcare are, by nature, observational field studies conducted by social scientists. Historically, these practices have neglected any follow-on analysis by economists, data analysts, or mathematicians. In this paper, we argue that the mitigation of failure demand can only be effectively navigated through analytical cost-benefit modelling conducted in conjunction with a comprehensive uncertainty-sensitivity analysis. Using an existing failure demand field study as the starting point, we demonstrate how such a follow up analysis can be conducted and formulate a pragmatic decision support methodological framework that can be disseminated to the researchers and practitioners throughout the broad healthcare field. The framework emanates from classical cost-benefit modelling that is then supplemented with Monte Carlo simulation in combination with the groundbreaking Simulation Decomposition (SimDec) method. The SimDec results reveal additional insights critical for decision making that could not be readily uncovered by any other existing techniques. While SimDec’s methodological framework is straightforward to implement using various open-source computer code packages, this paper shows how non-technical healthcare practitioners can easily conduct an entirely congruent analysis via the freely-accessible web dashboard interface or the downloadable spreadsheet template.

entry.title: Nonparametric Change-Point Detection for Modern Data: Representations and Statistical Guarantees

link.title: Nonparametric Change-Point Detection for Modern Data: Representations and Statistical Guarantees

entry.content: Nonparametric change-point methods for high-dimensional and non-Euclidean data, including networks and covariance matrices, compare observations through a representation: coordinates, kernels, distances, similarity graphs, ranks, or learned scores. These representations affect which changes a method can detect and what the reported evidence means. We review retrospective methods by relating their representations to the population discrepancies targeted by their scores, the search over change times, the calibration of that search, and the resulting statistical guarantee. We distinguish population identification, detection power, scan-level error control, and localization, and examine these guarantees for multiple changes, dependent sequences, objects estimated from replicates, and online monitoring. Simulation experiments illustrate these distinctions: two scores on the same nearest-neighbor graph have similar power but give different location estimates. These comparisons guide the choice of a representation that preserves the change of scientific interest and a procedure whose guarantee supports the intended inference.

entry.title: Asymptotically Efficient Conformal Inference for Individual Treatment Effects under Multivalued Treatments

link.title: Asymptotically Efficient Conformal Inference for Individual Treatment Effects under Multivalued Treatments

entry.content: Most existing conformal inference methods for individual treatment effects are limited to settings with binary treatments. For multiple treatments, propensity score-derived weights often suffer from statistical instability, while contiguous prediction intervals may span low-density regions between modes of potential outcome distributions, leading to inefficient prediction sets. We propose adaptive prediction sets for counterfactual outcomes under multivalued treatments by combining KuLSIF-based density ratio estimation with highest predictive density (HPD) conformal scores derived from conditional density estimates. Both estimators share a reproducing kernel Hilbert space least-squares formulation, which simplifies theoretical derivation and analysis. The resulting prediction sets are robust to heteroscedasticity and multimodal outcome distributions and effectively eliminate low-density regions between distribution modes. Under unconfoundedness assumption and regularity conditions, we prove that the proposed method converges to optimal HPD sets under covariate shift and establish its asymptotic conditional validity and statistical efficiency. Simulation studies and ACIC benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves empirical coverage probabilities close to the nominal level, while yielding shorter average interval lengths than conventional quantile-based conformal methods for multimodal outcome data.

entry.title: Breaking Resonance: Square-root acceleration for Metropolis-adjusted randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

link.title: Breaking Resonance: Square-root acceleration for Metropolis-adjusted randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

entry.content: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with a fixed integration time can fail to mix because of resonances, and randomizing the integration time removes them. We prove that Metropolis-adjusted HMC with velocity Verlet and random integration times mixes from a warm start in a number of transitions that does not depend on the condition number, for every integration-time law satisfying a Fourier condition that we call non-resonant; uniform, exponential and triangular laws are examples. For a target density proportional to $e^{-U}$ on $\mathbb R^d$, where $U$ is $m$-strongly convex with $L$-Lipschitz gradient and $L_H$-Lipschitz Hessian and $\kappa=L/m$, the number of gradient evaluations needed to reach a fixed total variation accuracy is, up to constants and logarithmic factors, $\sqrt{\kappa d}+\sqrt{L_H}\,(d/m)^{3/4}$. This is the first square-root condition-number bound for this sampler beyond Gaussian targets. The proof converts relative-entropy contraction of the unadjusted proposal into a conductance bound for the adjusted chain, and shows that the integration-time law enters only through its characteristic function. Hessian regularity cannot be dropped for a fixed step size: without it there are targets in the class for which the cost is at least of order $\kappa^{2/3}$, up to logarithmic factors, even from a warm start.

entry.title: Admissibility of Linear Time Series Models under Cone Constraints

link.title: Admissibility of Linear Time Series Models under Cone Constraints

entry.content: Time series analysis extends beyond vector-valued observations to evolving probability densities, quantile functions, and covariance operators. These objects carry intrinsic constraints, raising questions about the admissibility of additive linear models, which have long served as a foundation for time series modelling and theory. We give a necessary and sufficient support condition for a stationary Hilbert-space linear process to remain in a closed convex cone almost surely. Innovations with unbounded lower tails, including Gaussian innovations, confine randomness to the cone’s largest linear subspace. For fractional filters with convergent normalized cumulative coefficients, the leading stochastic directions obey the same restriction, even with bounded innovations. For real-line quantiles, variation under unbounded lower tails and leading fractional accumulation can occur only through location shifts. For cone-valued processes, partial sums of centred stationary increments remain bounded in mean square when evaluated by any linear functional that is nonnegative on the cone, in contrast to the growing variance of a random walk. We derive an exact slope criterion for locally absolutely continuous quantiles and construct nondegenerate additive models with bounded innovations for quantiles, densities, and covariance matrices. These findings clarify the scope of ordinary additive modelling under structural constraints.

entry.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs

link.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs

entry.content: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents’ hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $\beta\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\ge\beta$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR’s public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model’s 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.

entry.title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs

link.title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs

entry.content: Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation. CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.

entry.title: Partial Identification under Imperfect Compliance via Cross-World Correlation Restriction

link.title: Partial Identification under Imperfect Compliance via Cross-World Correlation Restriction

entry.content: This article develops a unified partial identification approach for the average treatment effect (ATE) and the local average treatment effect (LATE) in randomized experiments with imperfect compliance, incorporating the cross-world correlation between potential treatment statuses. Even under random assignment and exclusion restriction, the correlation is unidentified. However, given the two identified marginals, it uniquely determines the relative proportions of the four principal strata, with monotonicity corresponding to a special case. We derive explicit sharp bounds for both the ATE and LATE at a fixed correlation and extend the results to prespecified correlation ranges, providing a sensitivity analysis that incorporates substantive information about compliance behavior. For the ATE, the lower bound decreases and the upper bound increases with the correlation. Although imposing monotonicity does not tighten the conventional Balke–Pearl bounds, we show that restricting the correlation can yield tighter bounds, even when defiers remain possible. For the LATE, the sharp bounds may not vary monotonically with the correlation, and we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for point identification of the LATE at any feasible correlation value, with the conventional Wald ratio identification result under monotonicity as a special case. In addition, we derive a breakdown point for the correlation that determines when the Wald ratio falls outside the sharp identified set for the LATE. Applications to four empirical studies illustrate how cross-world correlation restrictions tighten the sharp bounds for the ATE and LATE and assess the breakdown of the Wald ratio.

entry.title: Simultaneous Inference for Watermark Proportions in LLM-Generated Text

link.title: Simultaneous Inference for Watermark Proportions in LLM-Generated Text

entry.content: Watermarking enables detection of text generated by large language models, but practical review also requires quantifying retained signals within content of interest. Readers may choose passages based on their content and refine their selections after examining the watermark evidence. We develop simultaneous lower confidence bounds on the fraction of selected tokens that retain a watermark signal. The bounds hold jointly for the full document and any passages selected during review. We develop structure-adaptive closed testing (SACT), which uses a working model of sequential signal clustering to construct scores for calibrated sign-based tests. Under a conditional null model, the bounds have finite-sample simultaneous validity even when the working model is misspecified. An exact reference-family representation recovers the full closed-testing bounds while enabling efficient repeated queries. In a constructed database-recovery review, SACT detects document-wide watermark signals and provides lower confidence bounds on watermark proportions in selected passages. Assessing related passages together gives a sharper lower bound on their combined signal count. In simulations spanning two watermarking mechanisms and a range of signal strengths and densities, SACT generally has higher power than competing methods.

entry.title: Adaptive Multi-kernel Correntropy Kalman Filter: A Variational Bayesian Approach

link.title: Adaptive Multi-kernel Correntropy Kalman Filter: A Variational Bayesian Approach

entry.content: This paper proposes an adaptive multi-kernel correntropy Kalman filter (AMCKF) for robust state estimation in the presence of heavy-tailed measurement noises and outliers. The multi-kernel correntropy loss is reformulated via half-quadratic (HQ) duality into a quadratic form with auxiliary weights, enabling efficient Kalman-like recursions. We establish a rigorous variational Bayesian framework under the mean-field assumption, deriving closed-form coordinate ascent variational inference updates for joint state and kernel width estimation. To enable online implementation, AMCKF is then proposed as an efficient single-pass approximation of the exact coordinate ascent variational inference (CAVI), where the state and auxiliary variables are updated iteratively via IRLS, followed by a closed-form kernel width update. A forgetting mechanism is designed to prevent over-confidence and ensure long-term adaptability. Simulations on target tracking and IMU attitude estimation demonstrate that the proposed AMCKF significantly outperforms standard KF, VBKF, Student’s t-based KF, and fixed-kernel MKCKF in scenarios with sparse outliers, heavy-tailed noise, and mixed disturbances, while maintaining optimal performance under Gaussian conditions.

entry.title: Model-Based Clustering of Longitudinal Functional Data with Hidden Semi-Markov Models

link.title: Model-Based Clustering of Longitudinal Functional Data with Hidden Semi-Markov Models

entry.content: Model-based clustering of longitudinal functional data must account both for heterogeneity among curves and for temporal dependence in their latent group memberships. Functional mixture models typically treat curves as exchangeable, while temporal approaches may restrict regime persistence or ignore state-specific functional variation. We propose hidden semi-Markov models for ordered sequences of multivariate functional observations in which each latent regime has a parsimonious, state-specific functional principal subspace, extending functional high-dimensional data clustering (funHDDC) to longitudinal settings. Gaussian, contaminated-Gaussian and multivariate-$t$ emissions accommodate atypical observations, and explicit state-specific sojourn distributions govern regime persistence, with hidden Markov models as the geometric special case. Estimation uses expectation-maximization (EM) and expectation/conditional-maximization (ECM) algorithms with segmental forward-backward recursions, and identifiability is established up to label permutations and spectral indeterminacies. In simulations, temporal dependence yields the largest gains when single curves are weakly informative; with robust emissions, state-specific subspaces outperform a global functional principal component representation; and explicit durations add smaller gains when regimes overlap and sojourns are non-geometric. Applications to air-quality profiles and smartphone activity recordings, evaluated on held-out years and subjects, show improved predictive fit and illustrate how apparent duration effects can reflect time-varying transitions.

entry.title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores

link.title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores

entry.content: The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.

entry.title: Regression calibration for logistic regression with correlated measurement error and multiple misclassification in covariates

link.title: Regression calibration for logistic regression with correlated measurement error and multiple misclassification in covariates

entry.content: Epidemiological analyses often suffer from covariate data quality issues: measurement error in continuous predictors and misclassification of categorical variables. Existing logistic regression correction methods mostly handle only one error type or a single misclassified variable, with limited tools for multiple misclassified categorical exposures together with correlated measurement error in continuous covariates. To address this gap, we extend regression calibration for logistic regression to jointly accommodate multiple continuous covariates with correlated additive measurement error and two or more misclassified categorical predictors. We build a unified framework integrating additive measurement error models and misclassification transition matrices, deriving the regression calibration estimator (RCE) using Kronecker product algebra. This computationally feasible approach extends naturally to more than two misclassified categorical variables. We evaluate RCE via simulations across varied misclassification rates, error magnitudes, sample sizes and effect sizes, comparing it with the naive estimator that ignores measurement error. We apply RCE to the EPIC-InterAct male case-cohort data to adjust for correlated error in protein and energy intake, plus misclassification in binary physical activity and three-category alcohol consumption. Results show that neglecting these error sources produces substantial bias and misleading inference for main and interaction effects in nutritional epidemiology. While the RCE is a practical correction tool, it treats validation nuisance parameters as known and does not account for their estimation uncertainty.

entry.title: Generalizing Couple-Randomized Trials Under Limited Overlap and Missing Partner Linkage

link.title: Generalizing Couple-Randomized Trials Under Limited Overlap and Missing Partner Linkage

entry.content: We study how to generalize couple-randomized trials when some couple types are absent from the trial and the target survey reports partner characteristics without linking spouses. Under an additive effect model with unrestricted partner-profile terms, the target average effect is identified exactly when the wife and husband margins assign equal mass to each connected component of the trial support graph. A specified interaction is identified when its alternating contrast around at least one cycle is nonzero. Without linkage, we obtain sharp bounds by optimizing over pairings consistent with the survey margins. A spousal odds ratio can narrow the bounds for a binary interaction. We derive joint bounds for an index-patient design, quantify bias from common shortcuts, and estimate effects and bounds using Bayesian dyadic multilevel regression and poststratification. In a worked example based on 3,826 Health and Retirement Study couples and simulated trial outcomes, an index-patient trial and an unlinked survey yielded a 2.93 mmHg wide identified set for the couple-average effect. Linking the survey narrowed it to 2.38 mmHg. Adding 300 couples without diabetes narrowed the unlinked set to 0.28 mmHg and yielded point identification with linkage under the fitted model.

entry.title: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections

link.title: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections

entry.content: Valid inferential models (IMs) provide frequentist calibration guarantees, but validity alone does not determine which construction is most informative. We study finite-sample efficiency through concentration risk, the expected volume under a possibility contour. For a smooth, fully identified association and a specified parameter-volume measure, a weighted Neyman–Pearson argument identifies the generalized fiducial density as the optimal score for minimizing cut volume subject to fixed-data auxiliary compatibility. The resulting maximum-specificity transform gives an explicit volume interpretation of the fiducial efficiency ceiling, which need not itself be sampling valid. We develop two approaches to valid construction. The first minimizes design-averaged concentration risk among single, data-independent auxiliary-compatible contours. The design measure prioritizes efficiency without requiring prior beliefs or restricting validity. The second localizes the parameter-volume score to candidate-specific contours, yielding a normalized, valid IM equivalent to sampling validification of the relative fiducial likelihood. A parallel sample-space construction recovers the ordinary likelihood-ratio IM; direct validification of the ceiling provides another repair. For the same association, exact, data-independent predictive contours share a common fiducial distribution as a saturating inner probability, while generating different calibrated confidence-region geometries. Design averaging thus selects an efficient member without changing the underlying fiducial law. Examples in a two-component measurement model and an exponential scale model illustrate the efficiency gains and show that sampling-valid repair can improve on the raw ceiling by leaving the fixed-data auxiliary-compatible class over which it is optimal.

entry.title: Statistical Process Monitoring of Functional Linear Models

link.title: Statistical Process Monitoring of Functional Linear Models

entry.content: Monitoring the stability over time of the relationship between a functional response and multiple functional covariates is important in many industrial applications, either because the relationship itself is the quality characteristic of interest or because it underpins a predictive model whose validity must be verified as the process evolves. Existing methods either assume the model estimated in Phase I to be stable and monitor the resulting residuals, or re-estimate its coefficients at each sampling stage, which requires several observations to be available at a time. In this article, we propose the regression coefficient function (RCF) control chart to monitor functional linear models (FLMs) in which, at each sampling stage, an individual observation of the functional response and an arbitrary number of functional covariates become available. The proposed method employs an exponentially weighted moving loss to sequentially update estimates of the regression coefficient functions and the intercept function, which are monitored through Hotelling’s $T^2$ and squared prediction error (SPE) control charts. A post-signal diagnostic procedure is also provided to support the identification of the source of the detected change. A Monte Carlo simulation study demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly against small and persistent shifts, and a case study on monitoring the relationship between the air/fuel ratio and engine state variables in an automotive after-treatment system illustrates its practical applicability.

entry.title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation

link.title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation

entry.content: Clustering is a foundational tool for exploratory data analysis across the sciences. We argue that clustering methods should be evaluated along four dimensions: fidelity to the data’s underlying structure, interpretability of the recovered groups, stability under data perturbations and algorithmic randomness, and scalability to modern scientific datasets. Yet existing methods rarely satisfy all four criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PHM-ensemble, a general probabilistic framework for multiresolution clustering that estimates the underlying data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits and subsequently constructs a clustering hierarchy through hierarchical merging of the mixture components. On simulated datasets and the MNIST benchmark, PHM-ensemble matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms in agreement with ground truth, produces more stable results across runs, and reveals complex underlying structures. Applied to 1.82 million peripheral blood cells from the Human Immune Health Atlas, PHM-ensemble achieves higher agreement with expert-curated major cell-type annotations than the Leiden clustering used in the original study (adjusted Rand index 0.965 versus 0.789), while requiring only half the computing time. Beyond identifying major immune lineages, it reveals biologically coherent relationships among cell types and resolves finer structure within individual lineages, uncovering subtypes and cellular states consistent with known biology.

entry.title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data

link.title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data

entry.content: Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch’s treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.

entry.title: Exact local queries for pseudo-marginal Markov chains

link.title: Exact local queries for pseudo-marginal Markov chains

entry.content: Local queries of a Markov chain can depend on past updates outside the queried components. For pseudo-marginal chains with Gaussian graph priors, we construct decision certificates from finite historical parameter ranges to settle updates before all neighbouring records are resolved. Under shared random inputs and exact arithmetic, the executor recovers the reference parameters, auxiliary variables and likelihood estimates for any prespecified finite query sequence. We bound conditional expected work, including likelihood evaluation, historical range construction and execution management. On specified path and grid families, we fix per-node history lengths and all other parameters in the work bounds. As graph size grows, expected incremental work stays bounded for certificate execution and grows linearly for the specified cached pointwise evaluator answering the same query. In controlled experiments, certificate execution is faster than pointwise and parallel Picard execution for sparse queries, whereas Picard is faster than certificate execution for full queries. We apply the method to positron emission tomography and Gaussian process classification of Landmine data. For a fixed numerical tomography posterior, certificate execution completes all queries of regional mean distribution volume within budget, while full execution completes none from the same initial cache. In Landmine, posterior summaries of the difference in log length scales between two sites agree across pseudo-marginal and ancillary augmentation samplers within estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty. Certificate execution resolves almost every scheduled update over the full query sequence.

entry.title: Certifying total-variation contamination by betting on trimmed kernel witnesses

link.title: Certifying total-variation contamination by betting on trimmed kernel witnesses

entry.content: Two laws share a common component after each discards a fraction $\alpha$ of its mass, a trimming, exactly when their total variation is at most $\alpha$, so the contamination level $\alpha^\star = \mathrm{TV} (P,Q)$ is the share of each population without counterpart in the other. We bound it from below from two samples on any space with a bounded characteristic kernel. The kernel mean embeddings of all such trimmings of a law form a convex region, the regions of two laws first touch at $\alpha^\star$, and in every direction a region reaches as far as a trimmed mean. The difference of their closest points, the witness, selects the trimming. We fit a ramp of the witness on part of the data and bet on the rest, at each level of a grid. The bound is valid at every sample size. The cut points of the tested level carry most of its finite-sample gain over an untrimmed witness, while refitting the witness at that level makes it consistent, gives its rates and returns the trimming. When a function of the kernel’s Hilbert space separates the parts of the two laws without counterpart, the bound is within order $(n\wedge m)^{-1/2}$ of $\alpha^\star$ on a grid of that mesh, which is minimax over such pairs. When these parts touch, a margin condition guarantees a polynomial rate for Sobolev kernels and a logarithmic rate for the Gaussian kernel. For the Laplace kernel on the line this guarantee is not sharp: the witness stays between its two cut points, and for densities that cross once, with a likelihood ratio bounded away from one off the crossing, the error on such a grid is again of that order up to logarithmic factors. No informative upper bound exists without assumptions. On the Right Heart Catheterization data, with confidence $0.95$, each arm must lose more than a fraction $0.35$ of its patients, if both lose the same fraction, before their covariate distributions can coincide.

entry.title: Pragmatic Deeply Debiased ML

link.title: Pragmatic Deeply Debiased ML

entry.content: Debiased machine learning (DML) combines a fitted outcome regression with weighted residuals to remove first-order regularization bias when estimating parameters such as average treatment effects, yet a second-order bias remains whenever regression and weighting errors align. For linear regression functionals, we target this second-order bias by training a strong learner to predict first-stage residuals from many covariates, yielding a one-dimensional (or low-dimensional) working model whose bias contribution is estimated on an independent sample. To complement this targeted search, we also analyze general kernel-based corrections, including covariate partitions and smoothers. We prove that deeply debiased ML is algebraically identical to ordinary DML evaluated with a post-hoc regression update that adjusts each scored observation using kernel-weighted residuals from the remaining evaluation observations. In our empirical and simulation studies, strong initial DML learners often leave the second-order correction small relative to sampling uncertainty, in which case the correction serves as a diagnostic check alongside sensitivity bounds for any remaining misspecification bias.

entry.title: Bayesian Learning of Spatially Heterogeneous Causal Structure in Spatial Transcriptomics

link.title: Bayesian Learning of Spatially Heterogeneous Causal Structure in Spatial Transcriptomics

entry.content: Spatial transcriptomics preserves the location of each expression profile, making it possible to study how gene regulatory networks differ within a tissue. Across regions of a tissue, regulatory relationships may vary and even reverse direction, so identifying the causal relationships in a specific pathological region can provide insight into therapeutic targets. We propose SpaDAG, a Bayesian method for learning spatially varying causal directed acyclic graphs. By defining the graphs on a triangulation of the tissue, SpaDAG allows each edge to have its own spatial pattern and even to reverse direction across regions. We show that the graphs nonetheless remain fully identifiable, and develop an MCMC sampler that explores them efficiently by reversing an edge over an entire connected region in a single move. SpaDAG outperforms competing methods in simulations with and without direction reversals. In a section spanning a renal cell carcinoma and the adjacent kidney, SpaDAG finds largely different relationships in the two tissues, with those in the tumor concentrated on genes associated with therapeutic targets. Between two of these genes, it identifies a relationship whose direction reverses across the tumor boundary, generating hypotheses about their region-specific coupling. Supplementary materials and code for this article are available online.

entry.title: Where the Model Frequently Meets the Road: Combining Statistical, Formal, and Case Study Methods

link.title: Where the Model Frequently Meets the Road: Combining Statistical, Formal, and Case Study Methods

entry.content: This paper briefly analyzes the working or default assumptions researchers in the formal, statistical, and case study traditions typically hold regarding the sources of unexplained variance, parameter values, functional forms, time, and external validity. We argue that these working assumptions are often not essential to each method, and that these assumptions can be relaxed in ways that allow multimethod work to proceed. We then analyze the comparative advantages of different combinations of formal, statistical, and case study methods, and offer advice on how to combine these methods.

entry.title: Average Causal Effect Estimation in DAGs with Hidden Variables: Beyond Back-Door and Front-Door Criteria

link.title: Average Causal Effect Estimation in DAGs with Hidden Variables: Beyond Back-Door and Front-Door Criteria

entry.content: The identification theory for causal effects in directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with hidden variables is well established, but methods for estimation and inference beyond the g-formula remain less developed. Previous studies have introduced influence-function-based estimators for broad classes of identifiable effects. When implemented through the observed-data density factorization, these estimators can require conditional density estimation and numerical integration, which can be statistically challenging and computationally demanding for continuous or multivariate variables. Prior work on related causal functionals has used sequential regressions and Bayes-rule representations of density ratios to avoid these requirements. Building on established identification and influence-function results, we make these reparameterizations explicit for effects identified under treatment primal fixability, Tian and Pearl’s necessary and sufficient condition for identification of post-intervention law, encompassing settings beyond classical back-door and front-door identification. We construct one-step estimators under alternative nuisance parameterizations and characterize how these choices affect robustness properties and nuisance-specific L2(P) product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and root-n consistency. The estimators accommodate data-adaptive machine learning for nuisance estimation. To address potential violations of the target parameter bounds by one-step estimators, we also develop targeted minimum loss-based estimators (TMLEs) that respect these bounds. Our robustness characterizations and sufficient rate conditions apply to both the one-step estimators and TMLEs. Building on prior efficiency theory for hidden-variable DAGs, we further develop modifications of our estimators that exploit ordinary independence restrictions. Implementations are provided in the R flexCausal package.

entry.title: The empirical discrete copula process

link.title: The empirical discrete copula process

entry.content: This paper develops a general inferential framework for discrete copulas on finite supports in any dimension. The copula of a multivariate discrete distribution is defined as Csiszar’s I-projection (i.e., the minimum-Kullback-Leibler divergence projection) of its joint probability array onto the polytope of uniform-margins probability arrays of the same size, and its empirical estimator is obtained by applying that same projection to the array of empirical frequencies observed on the sample. Under the assumption of random sampling, strong consistency and $\sqrt{n}$-asymptotic normality of the empirical copula array is established. The theory is illustrated by deriving the large-sample distribution of Yule’s concordance coefficient (the natural analogue of Spearman’s $\rho$ for bivariate discrete distributions) and by constructing a test for quasi-independence in multivariate contingency tables.

entry.title: Trajectory-based cycle-level pedestrian crash prediction at intersections: A novel non-linear link function for block maxima led Bayesian GEV framework addressing heterogeneous traffic conditions

link.title: Trajectory-based cycle-level pedestrian crash prediction at intersections: A novel non-linear link function for block maxima led Bayesian GEV framework addressing heterogeneous traffic conditions

entry.content: This study develops a cycle-level framework for estimating pedestrian crash risk at signalized intersections under heterogeneous, non-lane-based traffic. Existing approaches often assume linear relationships between covariates and parameters, oversimplifying the complex, non-monotonic interactions among motorized vehicles (MVs), non-motorized vehicles (NMVs), and pedestrians. To address this limitation, the framework introduces a non-linear link function within a Bayesian generalized extreme value (GEV) structure to capture how traffic effects vary. It applies extreme value theory through the block maxima approach using post-encroachment time as a surrogate safety measure, with each signal cycle serving as an analysis block. It also proposes a behaviour-normalized modified crash risk (MRC) metric to account for pedestrians’ habitual risk-taking behaviour in Dhaka’s mixed traffic. Seven hierarchical Bayesian models were estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation and compared using the deviance information criterion. Models with a non-linear link function only in the GEV location parameter fit the data better than their linear counterparts. Results suggest pedestrian speed is negatively associated with crash risk, while flow and speed of MVs, pedestrian flow, and NMV conflicting speed show positive associations, though all remain uncertain. The selected model’s MRC estimate was close to the observed crashes at a 93% confidence level tuned to this dataset. These results suggest that the non-linear structure adds flexibility for capturing the non-stationary and non-linear nature of traffic extremes. This framework is a step towards proactive identification of pedestrian crash risk and after wider validation, it could support adaptive signal control and safety interventions in mixed-traffic environments.

entry.title: Hyperbolic inference for treatment comparisons relative to a preferred direction: An application to astigmatism axes

link.title: Hyperbolic inference for treatment comparisons relative to a preferred direction: An application to astigmatism axes

entry.content: The paper compares two independent von Mises populations relative to a known preferred direction. An angular Fisher information calibration represents each population as a point in a Poincar'{e} disk. A signed score at that point combines the population’s mean departure from the medically preferred direction with its concentration. We test equality of scores using separate likelihood fits and an empirical sandwich standard error. At every fixed pair of concentrations the centered statistic is asymptotically standard normal, including when either population is aligned with or opposed to the target. The resulting test and confidence interval concern the Busemann score difference. Simulations show that rejection under the score null can exceed the nominal level at the smallest sample size and is closer to nominal at larger sizes. Proposed method has larger empirical power for alternative with score contrast, compared to the existing one. An application compares the transformed postoperative astigmatism axes for the SNARE and irrigating VECTIS procedures. The estimated score is smaller for SNARE, but the confidence interval for the score difference includes zero.

entry.title: Efficient and Debiased Learning of Average Hazard Under Non-Proportional Hazards

link.title: Efficient and Debiased Learning of Average Hazard Under Non-Proportional Hazards

entry.content: The hazard ratio from the Cox proportional hazards model is a ubiquitous summary of treatment effect. However, when hazards are non-proportional, the hazard ratio can lose a stable causal interpretation and become study-dependent because it effectively averages time-varying effects with weights determined by follow-up and censoring. We consider the average hazard (AH) as an alternative causal estimand: a population-level person-time event rate that remains well-defined and interpretable without assuming proportional hazards. Although AH can be estimated nonparametrically and regression-style adjustments have been proposed, existing approaches do not provide a general framework for flexible, high-dimensional nuisance estimation with valid sqrt{n} inference. We address this gap by developing a semiparametric, doubly robust framework for covariate-adjusted AH. We establish pathwise differentiability of AH in the nonparametric model, derive its efficient influence function, and construct cross-fitted, debiased estimators that leverage machine learning for nuisance estimation while retaining asymptotically normal, sqrt{n}-consistent inference under mild product-rate conditions. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed estimator achieves small bias and near-nominal confidence-interval coverage across proportional and non-proportional hazards settings, including crossing-hazards regimes where Cox-based summaries can be unstable. We illustrate practical utility in comparative effectiveness research by comparing immunotherapy regimens for advanced melanoma using SEER-Medicare linked data.

entry.title: On min-Storey estimators for multiple testing and conformal novelty detection

link.title: On min-Storey estimators for multiple testing and conformal novelty detection

entry.content: In a multiple testing task, finding an appropriate estimator of the proportion $\pi_0$ of non-signal in the data to boost power of false discovery rate (FDR) controlling procedures is a long-standing research theme, sometimes referred to as ‘adaptive FDR control’. The interest in this theme has been reinforced in the recent years with conformal novelty detection, for which it turns out that similar tools can be used in combination with any ‘blackbox’ machine learning algorithm. Nevertheless, perhaps surprisingly, finding a solution for ‘adaptive FDR control’ that is optimal in a broad sense is still an open problem. This paper fills this gap by introducing new $\pi_0$-estimators, referred to as min-Storey (MS) and interval-min-Storey (IMS), which are built upon the so-called ‘Storey estimator’. Plugging these estimators in the adaptive Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is shown to deliver FDR control both in the independent and conformal settings. In addition, these methods satisfy an optimal power property over any (regular) alternative distribution. The excellent behaviors of the new adaptive procedures are illustrated with numerical experiments both in the independent and conformal models for various distribution structures.

entry.title: A bivariate cure copula model with zero-inflated gamma frailty for right-censored data

link.title: A bivariate cure copula model with zero-inflated gamma frailty for right-censored data

entry.content: In biomedical studies, paired survival data arise naturally when two event times are observed within the same subject. Existing statistical models seldom accommodate both cure fractions and complex dependence structures. In this paper, we propose a novel bivariate cure frailty-copula model for paired survival data with a cure fraction. By incorporating a zero-inflated gamma frailty, the proposed framework simultaneously accommodates a cure fraction and continuous unobserved heterogeneity among uncured subjects. Dependence between cure statuses is modeled naturally via an odds-ratio parameter, while dependence between survival times conditional on frailty is captured through a copula. To provide interpretable measures of overall dependence in the presence of cure, we derive population-level rank correlation coefficients, namely tie-adjusted versions of Kendall’s tau and Spearman’s rho. For suitable choices of baseline marginal survival functions and copulas, the joint survival function admits a closed-form expression, enabling maximum likelihood estimation and likelihood ratio testing. Simulation studies demonstrate satisfactory finite-sample performance and favorable comparisons with existing bivariate cure models. In a real-data analysis, the proposed model is favored by information criteria. An R package, curecopula, implementing the proposed methods is publicly available on GitHub.

entry.title: Fast Training of Mixture-of-Experts for Time Series Forecasting via Expert Loss Integration

link.title: Fast Training of Mixture-of-Experts for Time Series Forecasting via Expert Loss Integration

entry.content: We propose a novel Mixture-of-Experts framework, referred to as Expert Loss Integration MoE (EliMoE), for time series forecasting. EliMoE addresses the optimization problem arising from small gating weights by incorporating expert-specific losses, which provide each expert with a direct learning signal independent of the gate-assigned weight. Specifically, the overall objective comprises the base forecasting loss and expert-specific losses, allowing individual expert prediction errors to directly influence parameter updates alongside the aggregate forecasting error. The framework also encourages different experts to learn from different temporal segments of the data. The proposed framework is further combined with a partial online learning strategy that enables efficient incremental updates of model parameters. By integrating expert-level loss information with partial online learning, EliMoE improves forecasting performance while retaining computational efficiency. Empirical results across five benchmark datasets from diverse application domains with different sampling frequencies show that the proposed approach generally outperforms state-of-the-art supervised neural forecasting models, including Transformer-based architectures such as PatchTST, as well as zero-shot time-series foundation models such as TimeMoE. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the expert-specific loss integration strategy, highlighting its contribution to enhancing predictive performance.

entry.title: Random weighting inference for linear regression under serial dependence of unknown form

link.title: Random weighting inference for linear regression under serial dependence of unknown form

entry.content: We construct confidence regions for a linear regression’s coefficients, with regressors and errors forming a stationary ergodic sequence of serial dependence not necessarily known. We weight the observations by random variables from an independent auxiliary sample and estimate the coefficients by weighted least squares. We prove the estimator to be asymptotically normal with the sandwich covariance if and only if the bandwidth shrinks fast enough for the weights’ randomness to dominate the score’s serial dependence. Wald regions have the nominal level, under short memory with the dependence left unspecified and under long memory with a non-normal least-squares limit. We derive a condition specific to the slopes and a bandwidth from consistent memory-order estimates, and identify the estimator asymptotically with least squares perturbed by independent noise. In simulations, we compare our regions with self-normalized, fixed-bandwidth, and resampled intervals under short and long memory, and we apply the method to daily wind speeds at Irish stations, a long-memory series.

entry.title: A Family of Quantile Functions Useful in Clinical Studies

link.title: A Family of Quantile Functions Useful in Clinical Studies

entry.content: Motivated by upper-tail quantile-domain summaries, we study the quantile-based effectiveness persistence function defined as the ratio between the tail mean and the quantile function. We derive statistical properties of this measure and consider a rational (M"obius) specification of the quantile-based effectiveness persistence function. Under natural boundary conditions, this specification reduces to a canonical form, in which remaining life relative to elapsed time is proportional to the survival odds. The resulting canonical family defines a two-parameter class of non-negative distributions through its quantile function. Various properties, including descriptive measures, L-moments, and quantile-based reliability concepts, are derived for this class. Estimation of the model parameters using maximum likelihood is also developed. The proposed family is illustrated using a real survival dataset.

entry.title: A Deep Zero-Inflated Model of North Atlantic Right Whale Presence To Support Blue Economy Management

link.title: A Deep Zero-Inflated Model of North Atlantic Right Whale Presence To Support Blue Economy Management

entry.content: Effective modeling of endangered marine mammal species, such as the North Atlantic Right Whale, is critical for balancing marine conservation with the growing blue economy. Passive acoustic monitoring data collected by autonomous underwater vehicles provide new opportunities for localized marine species detection and oceanographic sensing, but introduce complex statistical challenges such as zero inflation, imperfect detection, and intricate dependence structures. In response, we propose the Deep Zero-Inflated Bernoulli (DeepZIB) model, a deep statistical method which jointly models latent species presence and conditional detection probabilities while learning complex habitat relationships from heterogeneous covariate information. We establish theoretical results on the model’s structural properties and conduct simulation experiments to demonstrate its ability to recover underlying parameters and latent presence fields. Application to real-world passive acoustic monitoring data on the North Atlantic Right Whale along the U.S. East Coast demonstrates improved model adequacy and predictive performance in capturing the species’ dynamic and spatially varying habitat. We demonstrate DeepZIB’s ability to generate high-resolution, spatially and temporally varying presence maps, providing valuable insights for targeted and risk-aware management of blue economy industries, ranging from offshore and marine energy, to fisheries management and maritime transport

entry.title: Towards Fair Comparisons of AI- and Physics-Based Weather Models for Extreme Events via the Weighted Potential CRPS

link.title: Towards Fair Comparisons of AI- and Physics-Based Weather Models for Extreme Events via the Weighted Potential CRPS

entry.content: We study whether deterministic AI weather prediction (AIWP) models issue more informative forecasts for extreme weather events than deterministic numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. The deterministic model output is subjected to statistical post-processing via isotonic distributional regression (IDR), or EasyUQ, before the resulting probabilistic forecasts are assessed using weighted versions of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). This extends the recently proposed Potential CRPS (PCRPS) measure to focus on extreme outcomes. Since IDR exhibits optimality properties with respect to weighted versions of the CRPS, the proposed approach inherits desirable properties of the PCRPS, and, in particular, facilitates fair comparisons between data-driven and physics-based models when forecasting extreme weather events. We apply this evaluation framework to forecasts in the WeatherBench 2 dataset issued by the AIWP models GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and FuXi, with the ECMWF’s high-resolution NWP model serving as a physics-based reference. The forecast models are compared when predicting mean sea level pressure, temperature, wind speed, and precipitation extremes, defined as exceedances or non-exceedances of thresholds obtained from historical observation data. Across a range of extreme-event thresholds, including thresholds corresponding to record-breaking events, the ranking of the forecast models remains largely unchanged. We find that AIWP models, particularly GraphCast and FuXi, result in the most informative forecasts for extreme weather events across most settings, suggesting that AIWP models have the potential to outperform NWP models when forecasting extremes.

entry.title: Inverse Probability Weighting in a Post-Bayesian World

link.title: Inverse Probability Weighting in a Post-Bayesian World

entry.content: We present a rationale for the use of Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) in a post-Bayesian framework, in which the bias-correction provided by IPW in a frequentist context is reframed as a retargetting of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the statistical model and the true data-generating process. We provide a coherent argument in support of this approach, including theoretical results concerning convergence and properties of the generalised belief posteriors. We present examples demonstrating the utility of post-Bayesian IPW in practice: these include two simulated examples of inference under selection bias in the observed data, and a large-scale real-data example concerning systematic biases present in registry data when using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) to predict prostate cancer mortality. The empirical and theoretical results together show the utility of IPW to address classes of problems previously intractable within a principled Bayesian approach.

entry.title: Transferring supremum-norm rates and weak convergence of covariance kernel estimators to functional principal components

link.title: Transferring supremum-norm rates and weak convergence of covariance kernel estimators to functional principal components

entry.content: We show that $L_2$-perturbation theory can be used to transfer rates of convergence in the supremum norm as well as weak convergence in the space of continuous functions from covariance kernel estimators to the associated functional \rev{principal} components. As an application we obtain optimal rates of convergence in sup-norm, including minimax-lower bounds, as well as asymptotic normality for estimating the functional principal components in a discrete observational model with errors under fixed, synchronous design. The sparse to dense transition which has previously been observed for mean function and covariance kernel estimators also applies here. Surprisingly, eigenvalue estimation exhibits a discretization-dominated regime under sparse designs, too. Our results further apply to estimators of cross-covariance and long-run covariance kernels, as well as to covariance kernels of derivative processes. We also present results of numerical experiments in which we use the Nystr"om method to compute functional principal components and eigenvalues, and give an empirical illustration to series of daily temperature curves.

entry.title: Randomization Tests in Randomized Saturation Designs

link.title: Randomization Tests in Randomized Saturation Designs

entry.content: Randomized saturation designs are widely used to study spillover effects in clustered populations. In these designs, clusters are first assigned to treatment saturation levels, and units are then randomized within clusters according to the assigned saturation. This paper develops randomization tests for such experiments under several null hypotheses that arise naturally in spillover analysis. We first compare each unit’s untreated potential outcomes at two saturation levels: the partially sharp null requires zero spillover for every unit, while the bounded null imposes a prespecified upper bound on each unit’s spillover effect. Both hypotheses can be tested using a common conditional randomization framework that provides finite-sample validity. We next develop a finite-sample valid unconditional randomization test of whether each unit’s untreated potential outcome is nondecreasing across saturation levels. Finally, we study weak average-spillover nulls and show that our conditional randomization framework delivers asymptotically valid inference using studentized statistics. Simulations and an application to the Zomba Cash Transfer experiment illustrate the finite-sample behavior and practical implementation of the methods.

entry.title: Fitting the topology of synthetic particle systems with a novel graph representation

link.title: Fitting the topology of synthetic particle systems with a novel graph representation

entry.content: The shape and arrangement of particles in a material determine its macroscopic properties. The generation of synthetic data with varying particle structure, often represented as 3D voxel images, combined with simulation of macroscopic properties reveals structure-property relations. Most particle generation models focus on single-particle characteristics like shape and size. We aim at fitting the topology of the particle system using tools from persistent homology. However, the large size of the required 3D image data makes existing methods computationally infeasible. We bridge this gap by introducing a novel graph representation of particle systems and transferring the computation of persistent homology from the image domain to the graph domain. This yields a postprocessing method for synthetic images of particle systems, that is independent of the underlying generation method and improves topological and geometrical agreement with real particle systems while preserving morphological characteristics such as the particle size distribution.

entry.title: Forecast combination under temporal constraints: An application to day-ahead electricity prices

link.title: Forecast combination under temporal constraints: An application to day-ahead electricity prices

entry.content: Day-ahead electricity prices are forecast by many competing models and at several temporal granularities, from hourly prices to block and baseload products. The resulting forecasts suffer from two distinct problems: forecasts produced at different granularities are incoherent, as the aggregates do not match the averages of their components, and no single model is the most accurate in every market, period and level. We address both problems in one step by applying the coherent forecast combination framework, recently proposed for linearly constrained multiple time series, to temporal hierarchies. entry.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts

link.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts

entry.content: Reweighting source samples to match a target covariate distribution is a standard response to distribution shift when generalizing evidence across populations. It is well suited to deterministic, learnable covariate discrepancies, but can fail when source–target differences extend beyond covariate shift or when estimation of the density-ratio weights is unstable. We introduce a new model where the discrepancy between two population laws comprises a deterministic covariate shift and a non-systematic component, modeled as random perturbation of the probability space. This separates systematic shifts, treated as bias and corrected by reweighting, from random perturbations, treated as distributional uncertainty and reduced by dataset pooling. Under pure random perturbations, this principle yields Augmented Inverse Distance Weighting, which combines regression augmentation with variance-optimal dataset-level pooling and attains asymptotic variance no larger than exact covariate balancing. When both components are present, we develop Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting, which interpolates between AIDW and standard augmented importance weighting. Both estimators tradeoff sampling and distributional uncertainty via a distributional distance quantifying the strength of random perturbations. We establish asymptotic normality of both estimators and provide tuning and diagnostic tools. On three real-world multi-site datasets exhibiting diverse distribution shifts, the proposed methods consistently reduce mean-squared error compared with weighting baselines, and improve empirical coverage when covariate-shift adjustment alone undercovers.

entry.title: COMPACT: Spectral Adjustment Scores from an Exhaustive and Nonredundant Set of Invariant Relations

link.title: COMPACT: Spectral Adjustment Scores from an Exhaustive and Nonredundant Set of Invariant Relations

entry.content: Observational datasets frequently contain many baseline variables, yet investigators estimating causal effects may not know which variables to include in the adjustment set. Confounding information may also be distributed weakly across many variables. Propensity scores can simplify adjustment by reducing high-dimensional covariates to a scalar with binary treatment. Although the propensity score is the coarsest balancing score, this balancing property does not necessarily distinguish among causal structures relevant to adjustment. We instead examine all causal graphs among a candidate score, treatment, and outcome while allowing latent variables. Under faithfulness, we identify all unconditional and conditional dependence relations that remain unchanged when the treatment-to-outcome edge is added or removed, leaving treatment-effect estimation to the downstream analysis. Together, these relations define the smallest compatible graph class expressible through the relations considered. We then develop the proposed algorithm, which implements this criterion through a generalized eigenvalue problem whose score space targets the span of a treatment-balancing coordinate and a residual-outcome coordinate. We show that sufficiently informative proxies can recover this span without direct observation of the adjustment variables, characterize the resulting score-recovery and downstream causal-estimation errors, and establish bootstrap validity for the full procedure. Simulations and a real-data application demonstrate superior performance over several alternatives.

entry.title: Estimating Global Network Density from Snowball Samples

link.title: Estimating Global Network Density from Snowball Samples

entry.content: Many analyses aim to estimate a global property of a population network, such as its density, yet only a subsample of the network is observed. Ignoring the sampling scheme, and treating the samples as complete networks leads to biased inference. Although this selection problem is generally intractable, we show that it admits an exact solution for snowball samples drawn from Erd\H{o}s–R'enyi networks. We derive the exact likelihood of such a sample, showing that it forms a curved exponential family in the edge probability with a low-dimensional sufficient statistic. We obtain the maximum likelihood estimator that accounts for the sampling design, alongside valid confidence intervals constructed by inverting a test based on the exact sampling distribution, via Monte Carlo simulation. Simulations show that this estimator remains unbiased even when observing as little as 0.1\% of the vertices, with nominal confidence interval coverage. We further assess robustness to departures from the Erd\H{o}s–R'enyi assumption using scale-free and small-world synthetic networks, as well as a real Facebook ego network. We find that, while the corrected estimator no longer attains unbiasedness under these departures, it still substantially outperforms the naive alternative throughout.

entry.title: Bessel-Debiased Pseudo-Marginal MCMC for Generalised Bayesian Inference

link.title: Bessel-Debiased Pseudo-Marginal MCMC for Generalised Bayesian Inference

entry.content: Generalised Bayesian inference exponentiates a weighted loss, sometimes an integral estimated by simulation. Loss estimators generally give biased posterior weights which Pseudo-Marginal MCMC does not correct, and greater variability raises computational cost. We introduce Sign-Corrected Bessel Debiasing (SCBD), a signed pseudo-marginal method using independent block estimates from ordinary Monte Carlo or randomised quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC). The correction is exact for i.i.d. Gaussian block estimates with unknown variance. For non-Gaussian blocks, we bound the posterior error in total variation. Under regularity conditions, the correction improves the fixed-data Monte Carlo bound from $O(M_n^{-1})$ to $O(M_n^{-2})$, where $M_n$ counts loss-integrand evaluations per loss estimate. Suppose the RQMC variance for a block of size $B$ is uniformly $O(B^{-\alpha}(\log B)^{d-1})$ in fixed dimension $d$. With a fixed number of blocks and a learning rate proportional to the sample size $n$, a per-proposal budget of order $n^{2/\alpha}$, up to logarithmic factors, suffices to keep the leading log-weight variance bounded. Our examples show that favourable RQMC representations can inherit this budget scaling and that RQMC variance reduction complements Bessel correction. Once the block estimates have been formed, the Bessel correction comes at negligible additional cost. The correction is generic, straightforward to implement, and supported by theory.

entry.title: From priors to performance: enhancing statistical efficiency with Bayesian dynamic borrowing

link.title: From priors to performance: enhancing statistical efficiency with Bayesian dynamic borrowing

entry.content: One of the main advantages of the Bayesian approach to statistical inference is the flexibility in incorporating information from various sources, from expert opinion to historical data. Whereas the literature on Bayesian dynamic borrowing is rich, practical guidance for how to implement such methods is comparatively sparse. We thoroughly review the most common dynamic borrowing approaches for external data, including how to incorporate multiple historical data sets. We then show how these techniques can be used in practice, using publicly available software, to perform important statistical tasks such as model selection, average treatment effect estimation and prior sensitivity analysis. The aim is to make analysts more confident in their use of Bayesian methods to incorporate external data. All code is made publicly available in a companion GitHub repository (https://github.com/EzequielEBS/hdbayes-tutorial).

entry.title: Multiple Testing Of Composite Null Hypotheses With High Dimensional Count Data: A Local False Discovery Rate Approach

link.title: Multiple Testing Of Composite Null Hypotheses With High Dimensional Count Data: A Local False Discovery Rate Approach

entry.content: High throughput sequencing technology is routinely used to generate high dimensional (HD) count data. One objective is to determine which variables are associated with a covariate via the testing of multiple null hypotheses, say $H_m:\beta_m = 0$ for $m = 1, 2, …, M$ where each $\beta_m$ is a regression parameter. The standard approach computes a $p$-value for each null hypothesis and applies some false discovery rate (FDR) method to determine which null hypotheses are rejected, i.e. which variables can be discovered as associated with the covariate. However, even if data are well modeled'', this approach tends to provide a misleading list of discoveries in that someuninteresting’’ negligible associations ($\beta_m \approx 0$) are discovered, while other interesting associations are not. This paper formally addresses this issue using Poisson Mixture models and a Local FDR (PMLFDR) procedure for testing of multiple composite null hypotheses $H_m:\beta_m\in[-\epsilon,\epsilon]$. It is shown that PMLFDR procedures allow for consistently estimable expressions for overdispersion, provide asymptotically optimal FDR control, and are robust with respect to model misspecification. Simulation studies and real data analysis illustrate that PMLFDR procedures perform favorably compared to established procedures in that they a) are flexible enough to model most HD count data regardless of the technology used in generation b) allow for continuous and categorical covariates and c) yield more meaningful discoveries without sacrificing FDR control.

entry.title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data

link.title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data

entry.content: Neuroimaging analysis commonly involves identifying task-relevant brain regions and examining functional connectivity. These objectives are typically addressed separately, without a model-based framework. We propose a Bayesian distance-weighted Ising model that jointly quantifies regional importance for task-label prediction and functional connectivity between brain regions. The Ising model favors agreement between interacting labels. We extend it with region-specific interaction parameters and weights based on distances between functional signals. The parameters quantify regional importance for distinguishing tasks, while the weights measure functional connectivity through signal similarity between regions. Inference for this model is challenging because the signals may be observed on unequal time grids and the likelihood function contains an intractable normalizing constant. To address this, we use a basis expansion and an auxiliary variable Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply the method to functional near-infrared spectroscopy data from younger and older adults, comparing resting-state and task-related activity. The model reveals age-dependent patterns of regional importance and connectivity. Among younger adults, the left orbitofrontal cortex contributes more strongly to task discrimination than the dorsolateral prefrontal and frontopolar cortices, whereas regional differences are less evident among older adults. Older adults also exhibit greater bilateral connectivity between corresponding regions, consistent with reduced hemispheric lateralization.
